biografia.001:
Emili Godes Hurtado (Barcelona, 1895–1970) was a versatile photographer whose career spanned more than five decades. He worked in industrial, advertising, scientific, medical, artistic and film photography, while also exploring the creative possibilities of the image.

His career reflects the transformation of photography during the twentieth century: from his early years of technical training to the adoption of the languages of modernity and the avant-gardes across all kinds of professional commissions.

Despite this extensive and varied output, Godes never set about building an archive of his own work. Unlike other contemporary photographers, who organised and preserved their collections, his work became dispersed among commissions, companies, publications and institutions. The absence of a personal archive helps explain why he remains little known in some circles today, and why much of his work has had to be reconstructed from collections held in different places.
biografia.002:
Emili Godes was born in Barcelona on 14 April 1895, into a family connected with music and the arts. His father was a tenor at the Liceo and a choirmaster. Emili received musical training in singing and violin, and also developed an interest in painting and art books. This education helped shape a sensibility that he would later bring to photography.

At around the age of fifteen he began working as an apprentice at Casa Riba, one of Barcelona’s leading photographic establishments. There he came into contact with cameras, materials, laboratory processes and international technical publications.
biografia.003: Godes Hurtado family, 1920. Emili is first from the right.
biografia.004: Emili working in the laboratory at his home.
biografia.005:
During the 1910s he consolidated his practical training. After Casa Riba he went on to work at Casa Cuyàs, where he became head of the laboratory. The experience gave him an in-depth knowledge of photographic processes and of the technical possibilities offered by new equipment.

During these years he also began submitting photographs to competitions and developing a body of personal work. From the outset, his professional activity coexisted with a desire for artistic experimentation: photography was not only a trade, but also a means of expression.
biografia.007: Emili Godes and Antònia Diago with their children Montserrat and Jesús, 1924.
biografia.008:
In 1928 he established himself as an independent photographer, although he had already undertaken commissions on his own account. In 1927 he had produced an extensive photo report on Córdoba, its streets and monuments, work that already shows his interest in architecture, the city and composition.

He also documented the urban development and construction works on Montjuïc associated with the 1929 Barcelona International Exposition. During the 1920s and 1930s he also worked on reproductions of works of art, industrial photography, advertising and photo reports for institutions and companies. His relationships with artists, galleries and specialist publications brought him closer to the modern currents of his time.

The Exposition also marked a turning point: from 1929 onwards his interest increasingly shifted towards technical and scientific photography. In the 1930s he was photography director of the journal Arxius de l’Escola Superior d’Agricultura and collaborated with the Chair of Entomology at the University of Barcelona.
biografia.010: Urban development and construction works on Montjuïc.
biografia.011:
During the Spanish Civil War he collaborated photographically with the Comissariat de Propaganda de la Generalitat de Catalunya.

In 1938, shortly before Nationalist troops reached Catalonia, he took part in the filming of Sierra de Teruel, the film André Malraux directed in Barcelona based on his novel L’Espoir. Filming, much of it carried out at the Orphea studios, was interrupted by the advance of the war, and the film could not be released until years later, in France and under the title L’Espoir.

After the Republican defeat, he destroyed some of his negatives to avoid possible reprisals and had to process the documentation required to continue working. The war and repression caused a rupture and partly explain the loss of material from that period, which today makes it more difficult to reconstruct his work.
biografia.012: Advertisement in La Publicitat — Emili Godes Hurtado.
biografia.013: Parets del Vallès during the war.
biografia.014: French poster for Espoir · Sierra de Teruel, André Malraux’s film, on which Godes worked in 1938.
biografia.015:
In the post-war period he rebuilt and expanded his activity and broadened his collaborations. He worked for companies, laboratories, scientific institutions and medical specialists, producing industrial and advertising photography for firms such as Catalana de Gas y Electricidad, Coca-Cola, Laboratorios Esteve, Myrurgia and Osram, among others.

His friendship with Francisco García del Cid, Dr Antoni Puigvert and the Escola Superior d’Agricultura brought him closer to scientific and medical photography, close-up photography and photomacrography. He also developed a significant activity as a stills photographer and made three short films: Màgica Nit, La Calumnia and Todo es según el color….
biografia.016: The Godes Hurtado brothers (Josep, Ernest, Ramon, Emili and Artur) with Jesús Godes Diago, 1942.
biografia.017: Montserrat Godes, Emili Godes and Antònia Diago, 1949.
biografia.018:
During the 1950s and 1960s he continued working as a professional photographer for companies, scientists, doctors and film studios. He continued to process his negatives and prints personally in the laboratory installed at his home.

He was a professional capable of adapting to different clients, techniques and visual languages without abandoning his own way of seeing. He died in Barcelona on 20 February 1970, aged 74, while still working as a photographer.

index.001:
Emili Godes was a versatile photographer whose work spanned artistic creation, industry,
        science, advertising and film. His eye brought photographic modernity into all these
        fields, from Barcelona and over more than five decades.
index.005: Emili Godes working in his photographic laboratory, against a red background.
investigacion.001: This study approaches Emili Godes’s work through the presence of modernity and the photographic avant-gardes in his output. The research reconstructs aspects of his biography, locates little-known works and places his work within the photographic, artistic, technical and social context of Catalonia.

investigacion.003: The research was carried out by Laia Foix as the final project for the Postgraduate Diploma in Management, Preservation and Dissemination of Photographic Archives at the Escuela Superior de Archivística y Gestión de Documentos. It corresponds to the 2013–2014 academic year and was published within the documentary environment of the Institut d’Estudis Fotogràfics de Catalunya.
investigacion.004: It combines three lines of work: a bibliographic review, consultation of contemporary newspapers and magazines, and the location and study of photographs held by heritage institutions and private collections. It includes interviews with descendants, especially Maria Rosa Godes and Emili Godes Faura, and gives particular weight to primary sources.
investigacion.005: To contextualise Godes’s production alongside that of his Catalan, Spanish and international contemporaries.
investigacion.006: To complete his biography using family testimony, bibliography and primary sources.
investigacion.007: To review and locate work dispersed among institutions, private collections and publications.
investigacion.008: To advance the chronological dating and identification of his photographs, especially in less familiar fields (medical, scientific, industrial and advertising photography).

legado.001:
Emili Godes was recognised during his lifetime for his technical command, artistic sensitivity and ability to work across very different fields. He took part in competitions, exhibitions and juries, published images in specialist magazines and maintained professional relationships with artists, scientists and photographers of his generation.

His legacy, however, became dispersed among institutions, companies, publications and private collections. Since the 1980s, various exhibitions, research projects and heritage collections have helped recover a body of work far broader than what was publicly known for many years.

mirada_moderna.001:
Emili Godes’s modernity is not found only in the photographs he conceived as artistic works. It also appears in his industrial, scientific, advertising and film images: in the way he looks at a factory, enlarges an insect, reproduces a work of art or constructs an image for a company.

Through his contact with publications, photographers, artists and institutions of his time, Godes adopted new viewpoints and procedures without abandoning the precision required of a professional photographer.
mirada_moderna.002:
Emili Godes was born in 1895, in the final decade of the nineteenth century, on the threshold of all the technical, aesthetic and ideological changes that would transform photography. He belonged to exactly the same generation as those who drove those changes in Europe and America: Paul Strand and Man Ray (1890), El Lissitzky (1890), John Heartfield and Alexander Rodchenko (1891), Christian Schad and André Kertész (1894), László Moholy-Nagy (1895), Jacques-Henri Lartigue (1896), Walter Peterhans, Albert Renger-Patzsch and Edward Weston (1897), Berenice Abbott (1898) and Brassaï (1899).

In Barcelona he coincided with an equivalent generation: Pere Català Pic (1889), Ramon de Baños (1890), Gabriel Casas and Josep Masana (1892), Josep Sala (1896), Joan Porqueras (1899), Antoni Arissa (1900), Joaquim Gomis (1902) and Josep Maria Lladó (1903). Of these, Arissa, Català Pic, Lladó, Masana, Porqueras and Godes himself followed a similar path: the transition from Pictorialism to New Vision.

Rather than labels and rigid categories, the twentieth century is better understood in terms of tendencies, transversal languages and techniques, personal phases and evolution. Godes did not belong to a closed group or sign manifestos: he was a professional receptive to his surroundings who evolved in parallel with his contemporaries.
mirada_moderna.003:
Godes spent eighteen years as an employee in two of Barcelona’s leading photographic establishments: first Casa Riba and then Casa Cuyàs, where he became head of the laboratory. He did not become independent until 1928. Far from distancing him from modernity, those years of professional practice were his route into it.

The Butlletí de l’Agrupació Fotogràfica de Catalunya —of which he was a founding member— drew its articles directly from specialist foreign publications (Photo-Revue, La Photographie, Photo-Era), giving him rigorous training in the most modern techniques and equipment of the period. This was complemented by Revista Kodak and Revista Agfa, publications born from the photographic industry that promoted industrial and advertising photography and moved away from Pictorialist principles.

He also worked for avant-garde painters and sculptors, and for art galleries: reproducing their works allowed him to encounter the artistic trends of his time at first hand. He sat on competition juries alongside Narcís Ricart, Antoni Arissa and Català Pic. This combination —technical training, contact with artists and recognition among peers— enabled him to make the leap and create his series of macro photographs.
mirada_moderna.004:
New Vision emerged from Bauhaus ideas. It promoted new framings and viewpoints —high and low angles, fragmentation, close details, and forms of decontextualisation sometimes close to abstraction— as well as contrasts of form and light. Its aim was to reflect reality as we perceive it visually, not as pictorial tradition arranges it.

All these devices appear in Emili Godes’s work: displaced viewpoints, fragmentary framings, diagonals and close attention to the visual structure of objects and spaces. Godes did not belong to a closed group, but his work clearly documents his transition from Pictorialism towards the modern visual languages of his time.
mirada_moderna.006: New Vision: a top-down viewpoint, far above the object, and a close detail that crops the sewing box until it loses both context and scale. The thread crosses the frame diagonally and organises the image; the burlap background becomes a pattern. The camera looks from a position a painter would not choose.
mirada_moderna.007: Untitled (violin neck over a keyboard), c. 1930
mirada_moderna.008: New Vision: the camera is oblique and very close, so the keys cease to read as a piano and become a rhythmic succession of black and white. The neck enters diagonally and breaks the grid; contrasts of shape and light replace a descriptive view of the instrument.
mirada_moderna.009:
Photographers of New Objectivity sought sharp focus and unmanipulated photographs, aiming for a unity between photographic technique and the object photographed: flat light, small apertures, long exposure times and the photographer’s eye. Godes’s technical precision was not incompatible with artistic expression. In his scientific, industrial and art-reproduction photography, detail, sharpness and control of lighting also create a visual experience.

This is the movement with which he has most often been associated: as early as 1986 Marisol Farré devoted a degree thesis to him entitled Un fotógrafo catalán de la Nueva Objetividad, and in 1996 the exhibition and catalogue of the Departament de Cultura presented him as Emili Godes. Fotògraf de la Nova Objectivitat.
mirada_moderna.010:
‘If the proponents of New Objectivity arrived at this practice through ideas, Godes, by contrast, arrived at it through practice. […] Godes, who after 1929 feels himself to be a man of his time, puts himself at the service of science, industry and publishing culture, and does so in the most empirical sense without ever relinquishing aesthetic values.’

Daniel Giralt-Miracle, text for the Primavera Fotogràfica exhibition, 1996
mirada_moderna.013: New Objectivity: sharp focus from edge to edge, diffuse light without dramatic shadows and a frontal framing that fills the picture plane. The plant is neither interpreted nor idealised; it is described: the rosette becomes a repeated geometric structure, and beauty comes from exactness rather than effect.
mirada_moderna.015: New Objectivity: the open pod, isolated against a dark background and without any Pictorialist device —no soft focus, toning or intervention on the print. A small aperture keeps everything sharp, with a long exposure and side lighting that models each pea and reveals the fibres of the pod. An ordinary food, observed with laboratory precision, ends up looking strange.
mirada_moderna.017: New Objectivity: direct, unmanipulated photography in which raking light describes veins, wrinkles and fingernails with almost documentary detail. The body is treated like an object —matter and texture before psychology—: this is not a portrait of someone, but an exact description of a pair of hands.
mirada_moderna.018:
Camera-less photography was the avant-garde’s most radical experiment: writing directly with light, without lens or negative. Christian Schad, Man Ray and László Moholy-Nagy practised it from the late 1910s and especially during the 1920s. Godes came to it around 1930.

In his photograms, attention shifts from recognisable representation towards silhouette, transparency, texture and abstraction. The MNAC holds six, deposited by his daughter Maria Rosa Godes in 1997 and donated in 2005: mostly plant motifs, but also everyday objects such as scissors.
mirada_moderna.022: Photogram: made without a camera, by placing the branches and vase on light-sensitive paper and exposing it to light. What blocks the light appears white and the rest turns black, so the tones are reversed; the opaque vase becomes a flat grey silhouette while the finer leaves allow some light through. There is no negative, lens or viewpoint: only contact, silhouette and transparency.
mirada_moderna.024: Photogram: the scissors were placed directly on the paper beside an open-weave fabric that filters the light unevenly and prints as a grid across the entire background. The second, fainter silhouette reveals an exposure made after shifting the object. The tool loses its function and becomes pure form: photography reduced to its principle —an object, light and paper.
mirada_moderna.025: The camera made it possible to move close enough to an object to decontextualise and fragment it, turning it into pure form. A pair of spectacles, hands or a piece of fabric cease to be useful things and become visual matter. In these images, photography as artistic expression and photography as a practical tool can sometimes be distinguished only by the context in which they are published.
mirada_moderna.026: Las gafas y la pipa de Mondrian, 1926
mirada_moderna.029: Close-up approach to the object: the camera moves so close that the fabric fills the entire frame, without edges, scale or any clue as to what garment it belongs to. What remains is the weave —the zigzag of the threads and tiny fibres caught by raking light—: matter and rhythm. The useful object disappears and only its surface remains, very close to abstraction.
mirada_moderna.031: Close-up approach to the object: an open book, spectacles, a dried gourd, a pocket watch and a newspaper cone, brought together at close range on a table. None now serves its original purpose: they matter for their form, texture and the hard light that cuts them out. The cone’s shadow even becomes independent, an autonomous figure as prominent as the objects that cast it.
mirada_moderna.032:
Photomontage allowed Godes to construct images by combining and reorganising different elements. The process expanded photography’s documentary capacity and turned it into a tool for visual synthesis, particularly suited to industrial, advertising and propaganda communication.

His photomontages occupy the same territory as those of Pere Català Pic —the leading theorist of the new photography in Catalonia— and Gabriel Casas, who brought the technique into institutional graphic language during the Spanish Civil War.
mirada_moderna.036: Double exposure was used significantly by the Surrealists, although it also became widespread in other contexts. In Godes’s work it appears as a means of superimposing and displacing reality, and it takes on a narrative function in Màgica Nit (1945), where it helps represent the realm of childhood dreams and fears.
mirada_moderna.039: Two frames from the short film Màgica Nit, 1945
mirada_moderna.040: Here double exposure ceases to be a purely formal device and becomes narrative: the star and comet are superimposed on the sleeping child’s face, while in the second frame masks invade the face. The same process that superimposes objects in still photography serves in film to give visual form to dreams and childhood fear.
mirada_moderna.042:
In his images of insects, plants and other natural forms, Godes turns scientific enlargement into a visual experience. His aim is not only to show: he also seeks to produce surprise, estrangement and beauty. He explained it himself in 1955: ‘At lower magnifications, and already outside the strict field of science, it offers us an immense panorama of unusual artistic interest, where curiosity finds a source of inexhaustible surprises. Until now, my specialisation has been directed solely towards this latter aspect.’

He mastered these techniques through his work with the Escola Superior d’Agricultura, with which he began collaborating in 1927. Professor Francisco García del Cid described him a few months later as an ‘indefatigable worker who has known how to devote Sunday mornings to me, learning the basic problems of photomicrography in just a few weeks’. The photomicrography apparatus he used had been specially built by Casa Cuyàs, precisely during the years when Godes worked there. The long-repeated idea that he worked with rudimentary methods and makeshift lenses made from glasses and bottles therefore needs qualification: he started from sound technical knowledge and appropriate equipment.

The series took time to become public. Sebastià Gasch devoted an article to it in Meridià in 1938 with five photographs, and it was he who exhibited it in 1944 at the El Jardín gallery in a solo exhibition. This was followed by three articles by Carles Sindreu: El Español (1955, nine photographs), Diario de Barcelona (1956, ‘Monstruos insospechados’, three) and the magazine San Jorge (1963, ‘Monstruos en primavera’, nine).

Terminological precision: close-up photography covers reproduction ratios between 1:5 and 1:1, photomacrography begins at 1:1, and photomicrography is used when a microscope is required. Much of what he called ‘microphotographs’ are technically photomacrographs.
mirada_moderna.043: Paisatge a través d’ales de libèl·lula (landscape through dragonfly wings), c. 1930
mirada_moderna.044: Enlargement and composition at once: backlit against a marsh landscape, the wings work like stained glass. The venation can be read cell by cell with the sharpness required by enlargement, while the background dissolves —at such close range, depth of field almost disappears. The result is no longer an entomological plate, but an image in its own right.
mirada_moderna.046: Photomicrography in the strict sense: the specimen, mounted on a slide and lit through from behind, appears as a translucent silhouette against white, with abdominal plates, spines and even the claws on its legs visible. The leap in scale —from something almost invisible to a 35 cm print— is what turns a domestic parasite into one of those ‘unexpected monsters’ invoked in Carles Sindreu’s title.
mirada_moderna.048: Close-up photography, with a reproduction ratio close to 1:1: the bean and its pod fill the frame. Side lighting distinguishes three materials —the smooth skin of the bean, the cottony lining of the pod and the bright edge— while the dark background removes any reference to scale. Nothing now suggests that this is food.
mirada_moderna.050: The enlargement reveals what the eye cannot see: the scales on the wing, the ocelli and the hair on the thorax. But Godes does not photograph it on a laboratory plate; instead he shoots from its own height with the sky behind it, so the antennae stand out like two drawn lines. The same image serves both to document and to astonish.
mirada_moderna.051: For Godes, framing was never a neutral decision. The point from which something is photographed transforms its scale, tension and meaning. His high angles, low angles, close-ups and diagonals show a desire to construct the image, not merely record what stood before him.
mirada_moderna.053: The camera is almost pressed against the wall and pointing upwards. The extreme low angle makes the towers converge, distorts scale and turns the façade into a single body escaping beyond the top of the frame. This is not a view designed to identify the building, but to make its verticality felt: here, viewpoint is the subject of the photograph.
mirada_moderna.054: Géneros de Punto Rafel, spinning room, c. 1940–1950
mirada_moderna.055: The opposite case: the camera is placed on the axis of the aisle, at machine height. The two lines of bobbins recede towards a single vanishing point and the empty floor in the centre orders the entire image. An industrial commission resolved through a framing decision —where to stand— that turns the repetition of the bobbins into the subject.
mirada_moderna.056: Godes’s modernity is also built from basic elements: light, lines, surfaces, volumes and rhythm. In his photographs these elements organise the image and can turn a functional object, a plant or an industrial installation into an autonomous composition.
mirada_moderna.057: OSRAM shop window, Exposición de la luz, 1929
mirada_moderna.058: Here light does not illuminate the subject: it is the subject. The luminous tubes draw a radial fan inside a diamond, and Godes photographs it frontally, centred and symmetrically so that the geometry reaches the viewer intact. The challenge is technical —metering an exposure in which the subject itself glows and everything else is black, without burning out the tubes or losing the bulbs at the base— and the result stands on its own as form.
mirada_moderna.060: A studio composition made from almost nothing: a small horse figurine, a paper star and bands of light projected diagonally. The shadow carries as much weight as the object that casts it, the light and dark bands cut across the plane diagonally, and the top-down view eliminates floor and depth. Light, geometry and rhythm are enough to organise the entire image.
mirada_moderna.061:
Against the bucolic ideal of idyllic landscapes, the modern photographer seeks human activity. The city becomes a subject: the urban fabric, people as a group, concrete and glass buildings. And the urban night becomes a new stage, with streets lit by public lighting that more sensitive cameras and film finally make possible to capture. Brassaï published Paris de nuit in 1933.

Godes photographed the Banco Comercial Transatlántico shop window at night during the Exposición de la Luz of 1929: an illuminated sign, reflections on wet pavement and a streetlamp. It was an advertising commission —the lighting installation used OSRAM lamps— resolved with the same visual vocabulary that his contemporaries used for personal artistic work.
mirada_moderna.065:
Advertising photography demanded clarity, precision and the ability to turn a product into an appealing image. Barcelona experienced a notable surge in this field during those years: in 1932 the Institut Psicotècnic de la Generalitat was created, with an Advertising Seminar closely linked to Català Pic, and the I Salón Nacional de Fotografía Publicitaria was held at the Publi-Cinema premises on Passeig de Gràcia, opening with the lecture La fotografía moderna como elemento de publicidad. Godes took part with his photographs, which were singled out by the press.

While specialist magazines remained faithful to Pictorialist salon photography, advertising —a commercial commission— opened the door to modern photography. Godes applied rigorous framing, contrasts, geometry and particular attention to lighting. In an advertisement for Laboratorios Andrómaco, around 1936, the young girl is Maria Rosa, his youngest daughter.
mirada_moderna.069:
In the post-war years it was in film that Godes developed his artistic creativity. He had worked in stills photography since the early 1930s, particularly for the Orphea studios, so he knew the medium thoroughly. Multidisciplinarity was also characteristic of artists of his generation: Catalans such as Ramon de Baños, Josep Masana and Josep Maria Lladó ventured into film, as did Moholy-Nagy, Rodchenko and Leni Riefenstahl.

He directed three short films, all silent. Màgica Nit (1945), just over eight minutes long, mixes the excitement of Epiphany-night presents with childhood fears and uses double exposure to show the protagonist’s dream world. La Calumnia (1946–1948), nineteen minutes long, is more narrative: it uses extreme close-ups, high and low angles to intensify emotion. Todo es según el color… (1952 or 1953), around eighteen minutes long and scripted by Ángel G. Gauna, was shot in markedly urban locations —inside the stock exchange during a trading session, the port from the top of the San Sebastián tower, railway tracks— and alternates colour and black-and-white images to contrast optimism and pessimism.
mirada_moderna.070: Hay un camino a la derecha (Francesc Rovira Beleta), 1953
mirada_moderna.071: Film still shot in Somorrostro, with the real beach shacks in the background. Godes lowers the camera to the height of the child playing in the sand, lets the dune cut diagonally across the frame and places the two figures in the empty centre. The set is not a studio: it is the city the film wants to show, and a promotional commission ends up resolved as documentary photography.
mirada_moderna.073: In the Albufera, with the pole crossing the sky diagonally and the horizon line set very low, the still water doubles boats and figures: half the image is reflection. The scene is shot against the light, so the characters read as silhouettes. It is a production still, but the composition comes from his personal work.
mirada_moderna.075: Filming in Salardú, in front of the Romanesque church. Instead of photographing the dance head-on, Godes places himself among the musicians: brass instruments and the tenora enter out of focus from the left and form a frame, the dancers remain in the centre and the mountain closes the background. The viewpoint turns a production photograph into a photo report.
mirada_moderna.077: Shot by Orphea, it was the first Spanish film nominated for an Oscar. At the station, while waiting for the arrival of the film stars, the welcome banner crosses the frame diagonally and hides those holding it, while on the right the local residents look on with uneasy expressions and a sign on the wall reminds them that in the new Spain blasphemy is forbidden. Berlanga’s irony fits into a single film still.
mirada_moderna.078:
Emili Godes’s modernity was not a style reserved for his personal images. It also appears in the commissions he carried out for companies, scientific institutions, doctors, artists and film studios. His ability to meet specific needs without giving up his own way of seeing explains the profound unity of an apparently very diverse body of work.

The best example of this synthesis is his report on Laboratorios del Dr. Esteve. In 1942 the company opened its new headquarters in the Guinardó district, and the Arxiu Històric Fotogràfic del IEFC holds around a hundred original negatives by Godes that document the facilities in full. The final prints have not been located, not even within the company itself, where there was no record that these images existed.

It is a report produced during the harshest years of the post-war period, when ideological and cultural repression was at its most suffocating. Yet these photographs retain a freshness in conception, aesthetics and framing that brings them closer to the iconography of the Republic than to the aesthetic of the new regime. Better than any other series, they show the extent to which Godes had incorporated the modernity of the avant-gardes into his professional practice, far beyond photographs made for competitions.
mirada_moderna.079: Laboratorios del Dr. Esteve, ampoule inspection, c. 1955–1960
mirada_moderna.080: The commission called for documenting quality control; Godes resolves it in a modern visual language. Instead of a general view of the room, he arranges the women workers along a diagonal and allows the repeated lab coat, cap and luminous oval of the viewer to create rhythm. The only light that matters comes from the viewers themselves, while the filing cabinet in the background closes the frame like a grid.
mirada_moderna.081: Laboratorios del Dr. Esteve, production room, c. 1960–1965
mirada_moderna.082: Factory photography with the sharpness of New Objectivity: a high viewpoint and small aperture keep vats, reactors and demijohns equally defined from foreground to background. The tangle of shafts, pulleys and pipes on the ceiling forms a grid that closes the image from above. It shows exactly what the company needed to show and, at the same time, orders industrial disorder into a composition.
mirada_moderna.085: Classification of Emili Godes’s viewpoints based on the study «Modernidad y vanguardias fotográficas en la obra de Emili Godes» (2014), by Laia Foix. The research, attributions and comparisons with other photographers are hers; the selection of images and the writing of this page are by this website.

obra.001: Emili Godes’s work spans artistic creation, industry, science, advertising, film and the documentation of his time. Explore the archive by theme and decade, enter each project and open each photograph to view its record.
obra.intro.arquitectura_instalaciones: Architecture appears in many of his photo reports: buildings, factories, laboratories, scientific facilities, exhibition spaces and residences. Godes used the camera to explain how spaces are organised and how architecture can represent an idea of progress, efficiency or distinction.
obra.intro.ciencia_medicina: Godes’s relationships with scientists, doctors and research institutions led him to work with plants, insects, natural structures, operations and medical research. In these images, technical precision and documentary usefulness coexist with a strong visual dimension. His collaboration with Francisco García del Cid and the Escola Superior d’Agricultura was crucial.
obra.intro.experimentacion_fotografica: Godes explored double exposures, photograms, unconventional framing, contrasts, enlargements and close-up techniques. This category brings together images in which formal and technical investigation is the principal element.
obra.intro.foto_fija_cine: From the 1930s onwards Godes worked as a stills photographer, mainly for the Orphea studios. He documented scenes, shoots, sets, actors and production materials. Research has identified his participation in more than fifty films.
obra.intro.fotografia_artistica:
Art photography was a constant dimension of Emili Godes’s career. From his earliest work and competition entries to his Córdoba series, his images explore composition, atmosphere, light and photography’s capacity to construct a personal way of looking at the world.

This category includes only images conceived primarily as photographic creation, not every visually appealing photograph made as part of a professional commission.
obra.intro.fotografia_familiar:
Godes also turned the camera towards his own family. These images portray the Godes family during the 1910s and 1920s: portraits of his daughter Montserrat, his siblings and his parents, first communions, weddings, outings to Montserrat, the snowfall of 1924 and everyday life in the family home on Carrer Bertran in Barcelona.

The group includes stereoscopic plates for the Taxiphote and, as well as forming a family album, became a testing ground where he experimented with framing, light and portraiture using the models closest to him.
obra.intro.fotografia_industrial: Godes produced an extensive body of industrial work for companies and factories. His images document facilities, manufacturing processes, machinery, workers and products, but do more than record what is there: they organise space, study light and turn industry into an image of modernity and progress.
obra.intro.publicidad: Advertising photography demanded clarity, precision and the ability to turn a product or service into an appealing image. Godes worked for a range of companies and applied to these commissions devices associated with modern photography: rigorous framing, contrasts, geometry and particular attention to lighting.
obra.intro.reportajes_urbanos_documental: The photo reports on Córdoba, Barcelona and other settings show Godes’s ability to observe cities, streets, monuments, activities and social transformations. They are documentary images, but also visual constructions in which perspective, light, scale and rhythm matter.
obra.intro.reproduccion_arte: Godes photographed paintings, sculptures, ceramics, jewellery and other works of art for artists, galleries, publications and catalogues. This activity required mastery of lighting, tonal reproduction, scale and fidelity to the original, and kept him in direct contact with the artistic production of his time.
